questions.q: If the temperature of a gas is increased from $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $159^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$, the increase in the rms speed of the gas molecules is
questions.solution: RMS speed of gas, $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}}}\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad V_{\mathrm{mss}} \alpha \sqrt{\mathrm{T}} \\ & \text{ Initial temperature, } \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{i}}=27+273=300 \mathrm{k} \\ & \text{ Final temperature, } \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}=159+273=432 \mathrm{k} \\ & \% \text{ increase$ in $RMS speed }=\frac{\sqrt{432}-\sqrt{300}}{\sqrt{300}} \times 100 \\ & =\frac{20.78-17.32}{17.32} \times 100 \\ & =19.78 \approx 20\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the temperature of a gas is increased from $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $159^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$, then the percentage increase in the rms speed of the gas molecules is
questions.solution:
$V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}}}$ At $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}=27+273=300 \mathrm{ K}\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}_1}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{R}(300)}{\mathrm{M}}} \text{$ and $} \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}_2}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{R}(432)}{\mathrm{M}}} \\ & \text{ at } \mathrmT^{\prime}=159+273=432\end{aligned}\therefore$ Percentage increase in the $\mathrm{r} \mathrm{ms}$ speed
$=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{mms}_2}-\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}_1}}{\mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{rms}_1}}\right) \times 100=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{3 R}{M}}(\sqrt{432}-\sqrt{300})}{\sqrt{\frac{3 R}{M}}(\sqrt{300})} \times 100=\left(\frac{20.78-17.32}{17.32}\right) \times 100 \approx 20 \%$

questions.q: $\mathrm{N}$ molecules each of mass $\mathrm{m}$ of gas $\mathrm{A}$ and $2 \mathrm{ N}$ molecules each of mass $2 \mathrm{ m}$ of gas $\mathrm{B}$ are contained in a vessel which is maintained at temperature $T$. The mean square velocity of the molecules of gas B is denoted by $V_2^2$ and the mean square of the $\mathrm{X}$-component velocity of the molecules of gas $A$ is denoted by $V_1^2$, then $\frac{V_1}{V_2}$ is
questions.solution:
The mean square velocity of gas molecule is given by
$\begin{aligned} & v^2=\frac{3 K T}{m} \\ & \text{$ for $gas A, } \\ & v_A^2=\frac{3 K T}{m} \\ & v^2=v_x^2+v_y^2+v_z^2 \quad\left(\because v_x^2=v_y^2=v_z^2\right) \\ & v^2=3 v_x^2 \Rightarrow v_x^2=\frac{v^2}{3} \\ & v_1^2=v_x^2=\frac{3 K T}{3 m}=\frac{\dot{K} T}{m}\end{aligned}\mathrm{v}_1=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{KT}}{\mathrm{m}}}$...(1)
For gas B, $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}^2=\frac{3 \mathrm{KT}}{2 \mathrm{ m}} \mathrm{v}_2^2=\frac{3 \mathrm{KT}}{2 \mathrm{ m}} ; \mathrm{v}_2=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{KT}}{2 \mathrm{ m}}}$...(2)
Divide equation (1) by ( 2 ), we have $\frac{\mathrm{v}_1}{\mathrm{v}_2}=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{KT}}{\mathrm{m}}}}{\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{KT}}{2 \mathrm{ m}}}}$

questions.q: Air is filled at $60^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ in a vessel of open mouth. The vessel is heated to a temperature $t^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ so that $\frac{1}{4}$ th of the air is escaped from the vessel. Assuming air as ideal gas and the volume of the vessel remaining constant, then the value of ' $t$ ' is
questions.solution:
Initial temperature, $T_1=60^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}=60+273=333 \mathrm{ K}$ Mass of the air left in the vessel, $M_2=M-\frac{M}{4}$
=$\frac{3 \mathrm{M}}{4}$ Here pressure and volume remain constant from ideal gas equation $\begin{aligned}& P V=n R T \\
& P V=\left(\frac{M}{m}\right) R T
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}& \mathrm{MT}=\text{ constant }\\
& \mathrm{M}_{1} \mathrm{ T}_{1}-\mathrm{M}_{2} \mathrm{ T}_{2} \\
& \mathrm{ T}_{2}=\frac{\mathrm{M}_1 \mathrm{ T}_1}{\mathrm{M}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{M} \times 333}{3 \mathrm{M}} \times4 \\
& =444 \mathrm{ K}\\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}=\mathrm{T}_{2}=171^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas at $127^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is compressed suddenly to $\frac{8}{27}$ of its initial volume. If $\gamma=\frac{5}{3}$ for an ideal gas, then rise in its temperature is
questions.solution:
The condition for adiabatic process is $\mathrm{TV}^{\gamma-1}=$ constant

Before compression, $\mathrm{T}_1 \mathrm{ V}_1^{\gamma-1}=$ const.
After compression, $\mathrm{T}_2 \mathrm{ V}_2^{\gamma-1}=$ const.
Dividing (ii) by (i):

\begin{aligned}$ \mathrm{T}_{2}  \mathrm{ V}$_{{2}}$^{\gamma-$1}=$\mathrm{T}_{1} \mathrm{ V}_{1}$^{\gamma-$1} \\
& \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{ T}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{ V}_2}\right)^{\gamma-1}\\
 \mathrm{ T}_{2}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{ V}_2}\right)^{\gamma-1}\left(\mathrm{ T}$_{{1}}$\right) \\
 \mathrm{T}_{2}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V} \times 27}{8 \mathrm{ V}}\right)^{\frac{5}{3}-1}[400]=\frac{9}{4}$ \times400 \\
& =900 $\mathrm{ K}$.
\end{aligned}Change$ in $temperature,

\begin{aligned}
& \Delta$\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{T}_{2}- \mathrm{T}_{1}=900-400 \\
 \Delta \mathrm{T}$=$500  \mathrm{ K}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An insulating cylinder contains 4 moles of an ideal diatomic gas. When a heat $\mathrm{Q}$ is supplied, to it, 2 moles of the gas molecules dissociate. If the temperature of the gas remains constant, then the value of $Q$ is $\text{ ( } \mathbf{R} $$\text{ - universal gas constant) }$
questions.solution:
Heat supplied " $Q$ " is given by: $\begin{aligned}& \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{i}}\\
& \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{Initial}_{\text{Internal Energy }}\\
& \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{f}}=\text{ Final Internal Energy }
\end{aligned}$ Initially cylinder contains 4 moles of diatomic gas, $\begin{aligned}& \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{n} \left(\frac{\mathrm{f}}{2} \mathrm{RT}\right)\\
& \mathrm{U}=4[- \mathrm{RT}]=10 \mathrm{RT}
\end{aligned}2 moles of diatomic gas dissociate into monoatomic gas. Hence there are 4 moles of monoatomic gas and 2 moles of diatomic gas. Final Internal Energy is given by: \begin{aligned}
& U_f=n\left(\frac{f}{2}R T\right)+n^{\prime}\left(\frac{f^{\prime}}{2}-R T\right) \\
& =4\left(\frac{3}{2}R T\right)+2\left(\frac{5}{2}R T\right) \\
& =11 R T
\end{aligned} Thus Heat supplied is, \begin{aligned}& \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{i}}\\
& =11 \mathrm{RT}-10 \mathrm{RT}=\mathrm{RT}\\
& \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{RT} .
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Statement (I) : Gas thermometers are less sensitive than liquid thermometers.

Statement (II) : The ratio of universal gas constant and avagadro's number is called Boltzman's constant.

Statement (III) : The density of a given mass of a gas at constant pressure is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature.

The correct option among the following is
options: Statements I, II, III are true.
Statements I, II are true, but statement III is false.
Statements II, III are true, but statement I is false.
Statements I, II, III are false.
questions.solution:
Thermal expansion in gases is more than thermal expansion in liquids. Therefore, gas thermometers are more sensitive than liquid thermometers.

The ratio of universal gas constant and avagadro's number is called Boltzman's constant. $k = \dfrac{R}{NA}$

At constant pressure, $V ∝ T$& therefore, the density of a given mass of a gas at constant pressure is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature.

questions.q: If the root mean square (rms) speed of nitrogen molecules at room temperature is $100ms^{- 1}$, then the rms speed of Helium molecules at the same temperature is
questions.solution:
Nitrogen is a diatomic molecule and its molecular mass is ${M}_{N2} = 28g{mol}^{- 1}$.

Helium is a monatomic molecule and its molecular mass is ${M}_{He} = 4g{mol}^{- 1}$.

The rms speed of gas molecules at a temperature $T$ is given by,

${v}_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}} ⇒ \dfrac{vHe}{v{N}_{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M{N}_{2}}{MHe}} ⇒ {v}_{He} = 100\sqrt{7}ms^{- 1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylinder consists of a gas mixture of helium and oxygen. If the mass of helium is $4 \mathrm{~g}$ and the mass of oxygen is $32 \mathrm{~g}$, then the ratio of specific heat of the mixture $\left(C_p / C_V\right)$
questions.solution:
Mass of helium, $m_{\mathrm{He}}=4 \mathrm{ g}$
Mass of oxygen, $m_{\mathrm{O}}=32 \mathrm{ g}$
Helium is a monoatomic gas.
$\therefore$ Degrees of freedom, $f_1=3$
Oxygen is a diatomic gas.
$\therefore$ Degrees of freedom, $f_2=54 \mathrm{ g}$ helium contains $N_1=N_A=6.023 \times 10^{23}$ number of molecules
$32 \mathrm{ g}$ oxygen contains $N_2=N_A$ number of molecules.
(As atomic mass of oxygen is $16 \mathrm{ g}$ ) $\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad\frac{C_p}{C_V}$& =$\gamma\\ \text{$ and $} =\frac{N_1\left(2+f_1\right)+N_2\left(2+f_2\right)}{N_1 f_1+N_2 f_2}\\ \text{ and } =\frac{N_A(2+3)+N_A(2+5)}{3 N_A+5 N_A}\\ \text{ and } =\frac{5+7}{3+5}=\frac{12}{8}=\frac{3}{2}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperature at which the rms speed of molecules in hydrogen gas will be double of its initial value at $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is
questions.solution:
The rms speed of molecules in hydrogen gas is

$v_{\mathrm{rms}$}=$\sqrt{\frac{3 k_B T}{m}}$where,
$m=$ mass of hydrogen,
$k_B=$ Boltzmann's constant
and $T=temperature in $kelvin.

\therefore \quad v_${\text{rms }}$ \propto$\sqrt{T}$Initial temperature, $T_1=(27+273 \mathrm{~K})=300 \mathrm{~K}$
If initial rms speed be $v_1$.
Final rms speed, $v_2=2 v_1$ at temperature $T_2$.

$\begin{aligned}$& \therefore & $\frac{v_1}{v_2}$& =$\sqrt{\frac{T_1}{T_2}}$\\
& \Rightarrow & $\left(\frac{v_1}{2 v_1}\right)^$2= & $\frac{T_1}{T_2}$\\
& \Rightarrow & T_2 & =4 T_1=4 $\times$300 $\mathrm{~K}=$1200 $\mathrm{~K}$\\
& \therefore & T_2 & =(1200-273)^{{}^{\circ}} $\mathrm{C}=$927^{{}^{\circ}} $\mathrm{C}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A molecule is travelling in air at $300 \mathrm{ K}$ and $1 \mathrm{ atm}$, and the radius of the molecule is $0.6 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{ m}$. Calculate the approx. mean free path of the molecule. (The number density is $2.44 \times 10^{25}$ molecules $/ \mathrm{m}^3$ )
questions.solution:
Given that, temperature, $T=300 \mathrm{ K}$
Pressure, $p=1$ atm $=1.01 \times 10^5 \mathrm{ N} / \mathrm{m}^2$
Radius, $r=0.6 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{ m}$, diameter $d=1.2 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{ m}$
Number density, $\rho=2.44 \times 10^{25}$ molecules $/ \mathrm{m}^3$
Boltzmann constant, $K=1.38 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{JK}^{-1}$
Now, mean free path, $\lambda=\frac{K T}{\sqrt{2} \pi d^2 p} \begin{aligned}
\lambda$& =$\frac{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300}{1.414 \pi \times\left(1.2 \times 10^{-10}\right)^2 \times 1.01 \times 10^5}$\\
& =$\frac{0.2}{\pi} \times10^{-5} \mathrm{ m}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The following figure shows a Carnot engine that works between temperatures ${T}_{1} = 400K$ and ${T}_{2} = 200K$ and drives a Carnot refrigeration that works between temperatures ${T}_{3} = 350K$ and ${T}_{4} = 250K .$ The quantity $\dfrac{Q3}{Q1}$ will be
questions.solution:
Efficiency of Carnot engine is given by, $η = \dfrac{W}{{Q}_{1}} = \left(1 - \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}}\right) . . . \left(1\right)$
$⇒ 1 - \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{1}} = 1 - \dfrac{200}{400}, \left(∵ W = {Q}_{1} - {Q}_{2}\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{1}} = \dfrac{200}{400} = \dfrac{1}{2} . . . \left(2\right)$

For refrigerator, $COP$ is given by, $COP = \dfrac{{Q}_{4}}{W} = \dfrac{{T}_{4}}{{T}_{3} - {T}_{4}} . . . \left(3\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{\left({Q}_{3} - {Q}_{4}\right)}{{Q}_{4}} = \dfrac{{T}_{3} - {T}_{4}}{{T}_{4}}$
$⇒ \left(\dfrac{{Q}_{3}}{{Q}_{4}} - 1\right) = \left(\dfrac{{T}_{3}}{{T}_{4}} - 1\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{3}}{{Q}_{4}} = \dfrac{{T}_{3}}{{T}_{4}} = \dfrac{350}{250} = \dfrac{7}{5} . . . \left(4\right)$

On multiplying $\left(1\right) \text{ and } \left(3\right)$, we have
$⇒ \dfrac{W}{{Q}_{1}} \times \dfrac{{Q}_{4}}{W} = \left(\dfrac{{T}_{1} - {T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{{T}_{4}}{{T}_{3} - {T}_{4}}\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{4}}{{Q}_{1}} = \left(\dfrac{400 - 200}{400}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{250}{350 - 250}\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{4}}{{Q}_{1}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right) = \dfrac{5}{4} . . . \left(5\right)$

On multiplying $\left(2\right) \text{ and } \left(4\right)$, we have
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{1}} \times \dfrac{{Q}_{4}}{{Q}_{3}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{5}{7} = \dfrac{5}{14}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{3}} \times \dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{5}{7}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{3}} = \dfrac{2}{7} . . . \left(6\right)$

On multiplying $\left(6\right)\text{by}\left(1\right)$, we have
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{3}} \times \dfrac{{Q}_{1}}{{Q}_{2}} = \dfrac{2}{7} \times \dfrac{2}{1}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{1}}{{Q}_{3}} = \dfrac{4}{7}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{3}}{{Q}_{1}} = \dfrac{7}{4} = 1 . 75$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body cools from $70 ° C$ to $40 ° C$ in $5min.$ Calculate the time it takes to cool from $60 ° C$ to $40 ° C.$ The temperature of the surrounding is $20 ° C.$
questions.solution:
In the first case, the average temperature of the liquid

$= \dfrac{70 + 40}{2} = 55 ° C$.~
Excess temperature $= 55 - 20 = 35 ° C$

$\dfrac{d{θ}_{1}}{dt} = \dfrac{40 - 70}{5} = - 6 ° C{minutes}^{- 1}$

$- 6 = K \times 35$~...$\left(1\right)$

In the second case, the average temperature of liquid, $= \dfrac{60 + 40}{2} = {50}^{o}C$ .
Excess temperature $= 50 - 20 = 30 ° C$.
Rate of fall in temperature$⇒ \dfrac{d{θ}_{2}}{dt}$
$\dfrac{d{θ}_{2}}{dt} = - \dfrac{60 - 40}{tmin}$
$- \dfrac{20}{tmin} = K \times 30$ ...$\left(2\right)$
Divide $\left(1\right)$~by& $\left(2\right)$,~
$\dfrac{- 6}{\dfrac{- 20}{tmin}} = \dfrac{K \times 35}{K \times 30} ⇒ \dfrac{7}{6} = \dfrac{3 \times {t}_{min}}{10} ⇒ {t}_{min} = 3 . 89min$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The carnot heat engine have an efficiency of $50 %.$ The temperature of sink is maintained at $500K.$ To increase the efficiency upto $80 % ,$& the increment in the source temperature is
questions.solution:
Recall the formula of efficiency of Carnot's engine in terms of source and sink temperature,& $η = 1 - \dfrac{T2}{T1}$, here ${T}_{2} = 500K$, it means,
$0 . 5 = 1 - \dfrac{500}{T1} . . . . . \left(1\right)$ when the efficiency becomes,& $0 . 8$ then,&
$0 . 8 = 1 - \dfrac{500}{{T}_{1} + x} . . .\left(2\right)$

from the equation one and two,
$\dfrac{0 . 5}{0 . 2} = \dfrac{{T}_{1} + x}{T1} ⇒ 0 . 3{T}_{1} = 0 . 2x ⇒ x = 1 . 5{T}_{1}$
$⇒ x = 1500K$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a gas with molar mass $M .$~If the sound at frequency $f$ is introduced to a tube of~this gas at temperature $T$ then an internal acoustic standing wave is set up with nodes~separated by $L .$~The adiabatic constant $\left(\gamma = \dfrac{Cp}{Cv}\right)$ is
questions.solution:
Recall the formula of the fundamental frequency of the standing wave, $f = \dfrac{v}{2L}$, and the formula of sound waves in terms of absolute temperature and molecular mass,

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$,
$⇒ f = \dfrac{\dfrac{\gammaRT}{M}}{2L} ⇒ f^{2} \times 4L^{2} = \dfrac{\gammaRT}{M} ⇒ \gamma = \dfrac{f^{2} \times 4L^{2}M}{RT}$
&

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a two stage Carnot engine. In the first stage heat ${Q}_{1}$ is absorbed at temperature $T$ and heat ${Q}_{2}$ is expelled at temperature $\alphaT$ (where $\alpha < 1$). In the second stage heat ${Q}_{2}$ is absorbed at temperature $\alphaT$ and heat ${Q}_{3}$ is expelled at temperature $\betaT ( \beta < \alpha ).$& The efficiency of the Carnot engine will be
questions.solution:
The formula of efficiency of Carnot's engine in terms of sink temperature and source temperature is, $η = 1 - \dfrac{TSink}{TSource}$, in the two-stage Carnot's engine the source temperature is initial one and sink temperature will be the final one, it means, ${T}_{Sink} = \betat \text{ and } {T}_{Source} = T$
$⇒ η = 1 - \dfrac{\betaT}{T} = 1 - \beta$.&

questions.q: Mean free path of molecules in a polyatomic gas is independent of
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} \text{ Mean free path } & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2} \pi d^2 n_V} \\ & =\frac{\mathbf{v} t}{\sqrt{2}\left(\pi d^2 \mathbf{v} t\right) n_V}=\frac{\mathbf{v} t}{\sqrt{2}(V) n_V}\end{aligned}$
where, $d=$ size (diameter) of a molecule,
$n_V=$ number of molecules per unit volume,
$=$ number density of the molecules,
$\mathbf{v}=$ average velocity of gas molecules,
$t=$ time interval between two successive collisions
and $\quad V=$ volume of the molecule.
So clearly, mean free path depends on number density of the molecules, volume of the molecule, temperature of the gas (as average velocity of gas molecules depend on temperature of the gas).
But mean free path doesn't depend on gas constant $R$.

questions.q: If a gas has $n$ degrees of freedom, then the ratio of $\frac{C_p}{C_V}$ is
questions.solution:
For a gas with $n$ degree of freedom,
$\begin{aligned}
C_p & =\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right) \cdot R \quad \text{ and } C_V=\frac{n}{2} R \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{C_p}{C_V} & =\frac{\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right) R}{\frac{n}{2} \cdot R}=\left(\frac{n+2}{n}\right)
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an ideal gas, if the masses of all molecules are doubled and their speeds are halved, then the ratio of initial and final pressures of the gas is
questions.solution:
Pressure of an ideal gas is given by
$p=\frac{1}{3} \frac{m N}{V}\left(\mathbf{v}^2\right)$
When mass of molecule is doubled and speed is halved, pressure becomes
$p^{\prime}=\frac{1}{3} \frac{(2 m) N}{V} \cdot\left(\frac{\mathbf{v}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2}\left\{\frac{1}{3} \frac{m N}{V}(\mathbf{v})^2\right\}$
$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2} p^{\prime} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{p}{p^{\prime}}=\frac{2}{1} \Rightarrow p: p^{\prime}=2: 1\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Consider an ideal gas at pressure $p$, volume $V$ and temperature $T$. The mean free path for molecules of the gas is $L$. If the radius of gas molecules, as well as pressure, volume and temperature of the gas are doubled, then the mean free path will be
questions.solution:
Given, initial values of pressure, volume,
temperature, radius of molecule of gas and mean free path are $P p, V, T, r and L$, respectively.
$\therefore$ Mean free path,
$\begin{aligned} \lambda & =\frac{2 \sqrt{2} R T}{\pi r^2 N p} \\ \therefore \quad L & =\frac{2 \sqrt{2} R T}{\pi r^2 N p}\end{aligned}$
According to question if the radius of gas molecules, as well as pressure, volume and temperature of gas are doubled then
$\begin{aligned} \lambda^{\prime} & =\frac{2 \sqrt{2} R \cdot 2 T}{\pi \times 4 r^2 \times N \times 2 p} \\ & =\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{2 \sqrt{2} R T}{\pi r^2 N p}=\frac{L}{4}\end{aligned}$
(From Eq. (i))
Hence, the mean free path will be $\frac{L}{4}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel of volume $V$ contains ideal gas having mass density $\rho$ at temperature $T$ and pressure $p$. After a portion of the gas is let out, the pressure in the vessel is decreased by $\Delta p$. The mass of the released gas is
questions.solution:
Given, initial value of volume, pressure and temperature of an ideal gas in vessel, V_1=V, p_1=p $\text{$ and } T_1=T and density of gas $=\rho$
When, $\Delta V$ volume of gas is let out, hence pressure of gas is decreased to $\Delta p$.
Then, $\begin{aligned}& V_2=V-\Delta V \\
& p_2=p-\Delta p \\
& T_2=T_1
\end{aligned} By an ideal gas equation, $\begin{array}{rlr}$\frac{p_1 V_1}{T_1}$& =$\frac{p_2 V_2}{T_2}$& \\
$\frac{p_1}{p_2}$& =$\frac{V_2}{V_1}$& {$\left[\because T_1=T_2\right]$} \\
$\frac{p}{p-\Delta p}$& =$\frac{V-\Delta V}{V}=$1-$\frac{\Delta V}{V}$& \\
$\frac{\Delta V}{V}$& =1-$\frac{p}{p-\Delta p}$& \\
& =$\frac{p-\Delta p-p}{p-\Delta p}$& \\
\Delta V & =$\frac{-\Delta p V}{p-\Delta p}$&
\end{array}$ \therefore$ Mass of released gas $=\rho \Delta V=\frac{\rho \Delta p V}{p-\Delta p}$ \approx $\frac{\rho \Delta p V}{p}$

questions.q: A polyatomic gas has $f$ vibrational degrees of freedom, then the ratio of the specific heat at constant pressure to that at constant volume will be
questions.solution:
For a polyatomic atom value of specific heat at constant volume, $C_V=(3+f) R$ where, $f=$ vibration degree of freedom and $R=$ gas constant.
Now, $\begin{aligned}& C_p=C_V+R \\
& C_p=(3+f) R+R \\
& C_p=(4+f) R
\end{aligned} Now, ratio$ of  C_p and C_V$\frac{C_p}{C_V}=\frac{4+f}{3+f}$

\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}& =\frac{15.427-15.329}{15.427} \times100=\frac{0.097}{15.427} \times100 \\
& =6.34 \times10^{-3} \times100=0.634 \approx0.64
\end{aligned}
$

Volume $(V)$ is proportional to the length of hollow cylinder.
